newsitem.title: USA: Early lead concentrate TCs settled, zinc drags on.
newsitem.headline: Early lead concentrate TCs settled, zinc drags on.

text.p: Some early treatment charges have been concluded for lead concentrates as the zinc mating season looks set to drag on for a while yet before any deals are done, industry sources said.
A European lead source confirmed initial 1997 deals for lead concentrates "at a few dollars higher than last year" for a lead basis price of $600 per tonne.
The early deals represent a gain for the smelters.

"I think it has been easier in lead because the mines recognise there is some abundance in lead concentrates despite the Faro situation," the source said. "The surplus is mainly due to most lead smelters using more and more secondary feed."
Lead TCs for 1996 were settled around $170 to $175 per tonne basis a lead price of $600 per tonne - a sharp rise in favor of smelters at the time.
The lead concentrates picture was, unlike for zinc, clearer and encouraged quicker settlements, industry sources said.
"But we are expecting a bit more than a few dollars higher," said a North American lead concentrates buyer commenting on the early European deals.
"People are looking at settling bulk concentrates deals earlier as well - it's a relatively cheap source of zinc units," the buyer added.

On Thursday and independent committee reviewing Anvil Range Mining's Faro lead and zinc mine recommended that higher metal prices, 31 U.S. cents per pound for lead and 47 cents for zinc, were needed before reopening the mine.

Faro will shut on December 20 and milling will continue for a further three months. Officials close to the company said it was not clear if and how much lead concentrates will be available for 1997 contracts.
Normally Faro would produce 170,000 tonnes of lead concentrates grading 60 to 62 percent metal.
Traditionally lead TCs are settled after zinc.

This time round, however, a combination of a confused zinc concentrates picture - several mines have closed while the surplus that was widely forecast in 1996 never appeared - and the determination by zinc miners to win back ground which they felt was erroneously snatched from them in 1996 deals, looks set to prolong the zinc TC talks.
Zinc miners are offering $155 to $175 per tonne while smelters want to stick to around $190 where 1996 deals were concluded.
Mining and smelter sources said they expected no settlements in zinc before the New Year.
Thursday's announcement by ASARCO that it will reopen its Leadville mine in Colorado was not expected to alter the lead or zinc concentrates picture, mine officials said.
